content: Throughout Wikipedia, articles often include Chinese, Japanese, and Korean characters. Computers running English or other Western or Cyrillic operating systems may require specific configurations to properly display these characters. If these characters are not rendered correctly, it is referred to as mojibake in Japanese. If you see boxes, question marks, or nonsensical symbols instead of proper characters, your system does not yet support East Asian characters. Chinese Traditional Chinese text appears as it does on Chinese websites and Wikipedia. Simplified Chinese text appears as it does on Chinese websites and Wikipedia. Japanese Japanese text appears as it does on Japanese websites and Wikipedia. Korean Korean text appears as it does on Korean websites and Wikipedia. Instructions for Enabling East Asian Character Support Windows 3.1x, 95, 98, ME, and NT To display Asian characters in your browser, you need to download and install the Microsoft Global Input Method Editors (IMEs) for the required language(s). IMEs are system extensions that provide language support for English Windows systems when using Internet Explorer. If your system lacks the necessary character sets, select the with language pack option during installation. IMEs allow you to input Chinese, Japanese, and Korean (CJK) characters, while the language pack enables the display of these characters. Note that if you are using Office XP, the older Global IMEs will not work, and you will need to install a newer version specifically for Office XP. In some cases, your system may prompt you to download Asian fonts automatically when viewing pages in these languages. If not, you will need to manually update your system with the appropriate language support packs. Windows 2000 The process for enabling East Asian character support is similar to other Windows versions, but specific instructions are not detailed here. Windows XP and Server 2003 To install support for East Asian languages, you will need the Windows Installation CD-ROM. However, for Windows XP Media Center Edition (MCE), the CD-ROM may not be necessary, as some systems (e.g., E-Machines) include Asian fonts on the hard drive but do not install them by default. Windows Vista Windows Vista includes native support for East Asian characters, so no additional installation is required. Mac OS X In older versions of Mac OS X, such as version 10.1, you needed to install Language Kits from Apple to read Chinese, Japanese, or Korean characters on the internet. These Language Kits included WorldScript software, which provided encoding support for specific languages. Each language required a separate script. In more recent versions of Mac OS X, these Language Kits are included by default in all installations. Once installed, you can select the desired language character set for viewing web pages via the browser's encoding settings (e.g., View > Encoding in Microsoft Internet Explorer or View > Character Set in Netscape). Additional font packages are available on Apple's website. GNOME GNOME natively supports East Asian characters. KDE KDE also natively supports East Asian characters. If some characters are still missing, you may need to install specific language packages, such as `kde-i18n-ja` for Japanese. If issues persist, you can use the `qtconfig` tool to add a comprehensive Unicode font to your browser's font substitutions. Debian GNU/Linux To display Chinese, Japanese, or Korean characters on Debian systems, you must install specific font packages: Traditional Chinese (Big5): `ttf-arphic-bkai00mp` Simplified Chinese (GB): `ttf-arphic-gbsn00lp` Korean: `ttf-baekmuk` Japanese: `ttf-kochi-mincho` After installing these packages, restart the X server to apply the changes. Fedora Linux For Fedora Core 3, install the appropriate `ttfonts` packages: Traditional Chinese: `ttfonts-zh_TW` Simplified Chinese: `ttfonts-zh_CN` Japanese: `ttfonts-ja` Korean: `ttfonts-ko` For Fedora Core 4, 5, 6, and Fedora 7, the packages are named `fonts-Japanese`, `fonts-Chinese`, and `fonts-Korean`. Use the `yum` command to install these fonts (e.g., `yum install ttfonts-ko`). Gentoo Linux Enabling the `cjk` (Chinese, Japanese, Korean) USE flag enhances East Asian support in some packages, though it is not strictly necessary. Useful font packages include: `cjkuni-fonts` and `arphicfonts` for Chinese `baekmuk-fonts` for Korean `kochi-substitute` for Japanese For example, to view Chinese text, install the appropriate font package. FreeBSD FreeBSD allows the installation of CJK fonts through the FreeBSD Ports Collection. You can also install precompiled packages for this purpose. NetBSD On NetBSD and other systems using `pkgsrc`, you can install CJK fonts using specific commands. Slackware/Generic Linux Distributions To enable East Asian character support, download the appropriate TrueType font file (e.g., `kochi-gothic-subst.ttf`) and copy it to `/usr/lib/X11/fonts/TTF/`. You will need root privileges to perform this action. Then, run the following command as root: ``` /usr/X11/bin/fc-cache /usr/lib/X11/fonts/TTF/ ``` Restart the X server if it is currently in use. The new font should now be installed. Unicode Fonts Simplified and Traditional Chinese There are free font options available for both Simplified and Traditional Chinese. Additionally, Google Pinyin for Windows is a useful tool for inputting Chinese characters. Japanese A variety of free Japanese fonts are available for download. Korean Free Korean fonts are also available for use.
